draft.title: Millikan's oil drop experiment
card: Millikan sprayed tiny oil drops between two horizontal charged plates. Some drops picked up electric charge from the air or from X-rays.
He adjusted the voltage until a drop hung still. Then the upward electric force qE equalled the downward weight mg, so q = mg/E.
The drop's mass was found from its size and the density of oil. This let him work out the charge on each drop.
Every charge was a whole-number multiple of one smallest value, about 1.6 × 10^-19 C. So charge comes in units, and this smallest unit is the charge of one electron.
draft.remember: A drop hangs still when qE = mg, and every charge found was a whole multiple of the electron's charge.

a.q: What did Millikan's results show about the charges on the oil drops?
opts: Each was a whole multiple of one smallest charge
Each was a different value with no pattern
Each was exactly the same size
Each was a fraction of the electron's charge
a.why: The charges clustered at whole multiples of about 1.6 × 10^-19 C, so charge comes in units. A fraction of that value was never found, so charges were not any value at all.
a.clue: Look at what the measured charges had in common.

b.q: In Millikan's experiment, an oil drop of mass m and charge q hangs still between the plates in an electric field of strength E. Which equation applies?
opts: qE = mg
qE = 0
mg = 0
qE > mg
b.why: A drop that hangs still has zero net force, so the upward electric force qE equals the downward weight mg. Gravity still acts on the drop, so mg is not zero, and qE greater than mg would make the drop accelerate upward.
b.clue: A drop that is not moving has balanced forces.

a.best: Each was a whole multiple of one smallest charge

problems.detail: The why's last clause, 'so charges were not any value at all', is confusing. It reads as if the charges had no value. It should say the charges could not take just any value.
